questions.question: In 1848, who prepared a series of four prints visualising a world made up of 'democratic and social Republics'?
options: Giuseppe Mazzini
Duke Metternich
Frédéric Sorrieu
Otto von Bismarck
questions.explanation: In 1848, Frédéric Sorrieu, a French artist, prepared a famous series of four prints visualising his utopian dream of a world made up of democratic and social Republics.
questions.section: Section A: History (India & Contemporary World II)

questions.question: What was the official name of the Civil Code of 1804 introduced in France?
options: Napoleonic Code
Treaty of Vienna
Treaty of Constantinople
Prussian Code
questions.explanation:
Historical Context (Napoleonic Code 1804):
Napoleon Bonaparte introduced the Civil Code of 1804 (widely known as the Napoleonic Code) to modernize the French legal framework and dismantle feudal remnants.
Core Provisions of the Code:
1. Abolished all privileges based on birth.
2. Established legal equality for all citizens before the law.
3. Secured the inviolability of the right to property.
4. Simplified administrative divisions, abolished the feudal manorial dues, and freed peasants from serfdom.
5. Removed guild restrictions in towns and standardized weights, measures, and national currency.
This Code was exported to regions under French control, such as the Dutch Republic, Switzerland, Italy, and Germany. Correct option is (a).
questions.section: Section A: History (India & Contemporary World II)

questions.question: Which of the following measures was NOT introduced by the French revolutionaries to create a sense of collective identity (sentiment of nationhood)?
options: The notions of 'la patrie' (the fatherland) and 'le citoyen' (the citizen)
A new French tricolour flag replacing the former royal standard
Adoption of a centralized administrative system with uniform laws for all citizens
Continuation of the traditional royal white flag of the Bourbon monarchy
questions.explanation:
National Identity Measures in the French Revolution:
To forge a collective national consciousness ('sentiment de nation'), French revolutionaries introduced deliberate political and cultural symbols:
• Promoted the ideas of 'la patrie' (the fatherland) and 'le citoyen' (the citizen), emphasizing a united community enjoying equal constitutional rights.
• Replaced the former royal white banner with a new French tricolour (blue, white, red) flag.
• The Estates General was elected by the body of active citizens and renamed the National Assembly.
• Formulated uniform laws for all citizens within its territory and abolished internal customs duties.
• Discouraged regional dialects and made French the national lingua franca.
Hence, continuing the royal white standard of the Bourbon monarchy was explicitly NOT done—it was discarded as a symbol of royal absolutism. Correct option is (d).
questions.section: Section A: History (India & Contemporary World II)

questions.question: Assertion (A): The French Revolution of 1789 proclaimed that it was the people who would henceforth constitute the nation and shape its destiny.\nReason (R): It transferred sovereignty from the absolute monarch to a body of French citizens.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
(A) is true, but (R) is false.
(A) is false, but (R) is true.
questions.explanation: The French Revolution marked the first clear expression of nationalism by terminating absolute royal sovereignty and vesting political sovereignty in the collective citizens of France. Both statements are true and (R) explains (A).
questions.section: Section A: History (India & Contemporary World II)

questions.question: In which month and year did Mahatma Gandhi return to India from South Africa?
options: October 1914
April 1916
January 1915
March 1917
questions.explanation:
Gandhian Chronology:
Mahatma Gandhi returned to India from South Africa in January 1915.
Historical Significance:
In South Africa, Gandhi had spent over two decades developing and refining his novel method of mass agitation based on truth and non-violence, which he called 'Satyagraha'. He successfully organized Indian immigrants against racist registration laws and poll taxes.
Upon arriving in India in January 1915, on the advice of his political mentor Gopal Krishna Gokhale, Gandhi spent his first year travelling across the subcontinent to understand the conditions and grievances of the Indian masses before launching any political campaign. Correct option is (c).
questions.section: Section A: History (India & Contemporary World II)

questions.question: Mahatma Gandhi organized his first successful Satyagraha in India in 1917 at Champaran (Bihar) to support peasants against:
options: High revenue demands during famine
The oppressive indigo plantation system
Low wages in cotton textile mills
The British Salt Law monopoly
questions.explanation:
Champaran Satyagraha 1917 Context:
In 1917, Mahatma Gandhi travelled to the Champaran district of Bihar after being persuaded by a local farmer, Raj Kumar Shukla, to investigate the plight of sharecroppers.
The Grievance: European planters enforced the oppressive 'Tinkathia' system, which legally mandated peasant farmers to cultivate indigo on 3/20th of their total landholdings. When synthetic German chemical dyes rendered natural indigo unprofitable, planters extracted exorbitant illegal rents and compensations to release peasants from agreements.
Gandhi organized non-violent peasant resistance, faced down arrest warrants, and secured an official inquiry committee that refunded 25% of the extracted money. This marked Gandhi's first nationwide triumph of Satyagraha in India. Correct option is (b).
questions.section: Section A: History (India & Contemporary World II)

questions.subtopic: Economic Impact of First World War
questions.question: Between 1913 and 1918 in India, how much did the prices of essential commodities increase due to war financing and increased taxes?
options: Prices doubled
Prices tripled
Prices increased by 25%
Prices remained stable
questions.explanation:
First World War Economic Fallout on India (1913–1918):
During the First World War, the British colonial administration financed massive imperial war expenditures by floating war loans and sharply increasing domestic taxes in India (customs duties were raised and income tax was introduced for the first time).
Price Inflation: Between 1913 and 1918, market prices of essential food grains and commodities doubled. This triggered catastrophic inflation, black marketing, and severe deprivation for rural peasants and urban working classes.
Compounded Distress: This economic misery was exacerbated in 1918–19 and 1920–21 by catastrophic crop failures across many parts of India, accompanied by the 1918 influenza epidemic in which 12 to 13 million people perished (1921 Census). Correct option is (a).
questions.section: Section A: History (India & Contemporary World II)

questions.question: According to the Census of 1921, how many people perished across India as a combined result of famines and the devastating influenza epidemic?
options: 5 to 6 million people
20 to 25 million people
1 to 2 million people
12 to 13 million people
questions.explanation: The 1921 Census estimated that between 12 and 13 million people died in India as a result of severe crop failures, famines, and the 1918-1919 influenza epidemic.
questions.section: Section A: History (India & Contemporary World II)

questions.question: Assertion (A): Satyagraha was not physical force, but pure soul-force.\nReason (R): In the struggle, truth and non-violence were the sole weapons; a satyagrahi sought to appeal to the oppressor's conscience without malice or hatred.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
(A) is true, but (R) is false.
(A) is false, but (R) is true.
questions.explanation: Mahatma Gandhi emphasized that satyagraha was not passive resistance of the weak, but active soul-force grounded in truth (Satya) and love (Ahimsa), seeking to win over the adversary through suffering and moral truth. Both are true and (R) explains (A).
questions.section: Section A: History (India & Contemporary World II)

questions.question: What were the 'Silk Routes' that linked distant parts of the pre-modern world?
options: Underground escape tunnels built during the Crusades
Rail lines constructed by the British in China
Maritime routes used exclusively for transporting raw silk from India to America
Vibrant trade and cultural networks connecting Asia with Europe and Northern Africa
questions.explanation: Silk routes were extensive land and sea trade networks that knit together vast regions of Asia with Europe and Northern Africa from ancient times to the modern era.
questions.section: Section A: History (India & Contemporary World II)

questions.question: Which common food crops were introduced to Europe and Asia only after Christopher Columbus accidentally discovered the Americas?
options: Wheat, rice, and barley
Potatoes, soya, groundnuts, maize, tomatoes, and chillies
Sugarcane, tea, and coffee
Cotton, jute, and indigo
questions.explanation: Many of our common food staples like potatoes, soya, groundnuts, maize, tomatoes, chillies, and sweet potatoes originated from America's indigenous inhabitants and were introduced after Columbus.
questions.section: Section A: History (India & Contemporary World II)

questions.question: Archaeological evidence shows that cowries (seashells used as currency) from the Maldives travelled in the pre-modern world as far as:
options: Scandinavia and Greenland
North America and Canada
China and East Africa
Australia and New Zealand
questions.explanation: Archaeological finds reveal that cowrie shells from the Maldives were used as a medium of exchange and reached distant markets in China and East Africa for over a thousand years.
questions.section: Section A: History (India & Contemporary World II)

questions.question: Assertion (A): Silk routes are a good example of vibrant pre-modern trade and cultural links between distant parts of the world.\nReason (R): Historians have identified several silk routes over land and by sea, knitting together vast regions of Asia with Europe and northern Africa.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
(A) is true, but (R) is false.
(A) is false, but (R) is true.
questions.explanation: Silk routes carried not only Chinese silk and pottery and Indian spices, but also ideas, religions (Buddhism, Christianity, Islam), and travellers across Eurasia. Both statements are true and (R) explains (A).
questions.section: Section A: History (India & Contemporary World II)

questions.question: What does the term 'proto-industrialisation' refer to?
options: The phase of industrialisation before factories began to appear, characterized by large-scale decentralized production for international markets
The phase of space exploration and computer automation
The decline of agriculture and return to hunting-gathering
The establishment of cottage craft shops inside royal palaces
questions.explanation: Historians refer to 'proto-industrialisation' as the phase of industrial production prior to modern factories, where goods were produced by peasant households in the countryside for international merchants.
questions.section: Section A: History (India & Contemporary World II)

questions.question: Why did merchants from European towns begin moving to the countryside in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries?
options: Towns were completely destroyed by volcanic eruptions
Peasants in villages had invented steam engines
Merchants were legally banished from cities by royal decrees
Urban craft and trade guilds were powerful in towns and restricted the entry of new producers
questions.explanation: In towns, powerful craft guilds maintained monopolies, regulated prices, and restricted new competition. Merchants therefore moved to the countryside, advancing money to poor peasants to produce textiles.
questions.section: Section A: History (India & Contemporary World II)

questions.question: In pre-industrial rural England, why were cottagers and poor peasants eager to work for urban merchant clothiers?
options: They were legally forbidden from farming wheat
Open fields were disappearing and commons were being enclosed, so small plots could not generate enough livelihood without supplementary wage work
They wanted to migrate permanently to London to become actors
Peasant households had no children or family members to support
questions.explanation: With the enclosure of common pastures and loss of customary foraging rights, poor peasants could no longer survive on their tiny farm plots alone. Advances from merchants allowed whole families to earn cash wages without leaving their villages.
questions.section: Section A: History (India & Contemporary World II)

questions.question: Assertion (A): Even before factories began to appear in England and Europe, there was large-scale industrial production for an international market.\nReason (R): This phase of industrial history is referred to by historians as proto-industrialisation, and it was based entirely in rural cottage households rather than factories.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
(A) is true, but (R) is false.
(A) is false, but (R) is true.
questions.explanation: Proto-industrialisation demonstrated that industrial manufacturing for global markets existed long before mechanized urban factories emerged, organized across rural cottage networks. Both are true and (R) explains (A).
questions.section: Section A: History (India & Contemporary World II)

questions.question: What is the oldest printed book of Japan, printed in AD 868 containing six sheets of text and woodcut illustrations?
options: Tale of Genji
Bible
Buddhist Diamond Sutra
Ukiyo-e Chronicles
questions.explanation:
History of Print in Japan:
Buddhist missionaries from China introduced hand-printing technology (woodblock printing) into Japan around AD 768–770.
The Buddhist Diamond Sutra (AD 868):
The oldest surviving printed Japanese book is the Buddhist Diamond Sutra, printed in AD 868. It consists of six sheets of accordion-folded paper printed with woodblocks, containing sacred Buddhist sutra text and detailed woodcut depictions of the Buddha preaching to his assembly.
Later Developments: Printing diversified to include playing cards, paper money, and Edo period illustrated novels and Ukiyo-e woodblock prints by artists like Kitagawa Utamaro. Correct option is (c).
questions.section: Section A: History (India & Contemporary World II)

questions.question: In imperial China, traditional woodblock printed books were folded and stitched at the side as an 'accordion book' because:
options: Chinese calligraphy characters could only be read horizontally
Emperors ordered that all books must look like musical instruments
Glue was legally prohibited in Chinese publishing
The porous and thin paper could not be printed on both sides
questions.explanation: Because traditional Chinese paper was thin and porous, ink seeped through, making two-sided printing impossible; therefore sheets were folded and bound as accordion books.
questions.section: Section A: History (India & Contemporary World II)

questions.question: Assertion (A): Print culture was directly responsible for ushering in the Protestant Reformation in Europe.\nReason (R): Martin Luther's writings, including his Ninety-Five Theses and German translation of the New Testament, were rapidly printed and read by thousands, challenging papal authority.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
(A) is true, but (R) is false.
(A) is false, but (R) is true.
questions.explanation: Print allowed Luther's radical ideas to bypass Catholic Church monopolies and reach believers across Europe within weeks, igniting the Protestant Reformation. Both statements are true and (R) explains (A).
questions.section: Section A: History (India & Contemporary World II)

questions.question: An object or element in the environment becomes a resource only when it is:
options: Found in unlimited abundance in deep oceans
Manufactured exclusively inside government factories
Technologically accessible, economically feasible, and culturally acceptable
Certified by international patent offices
questions.explanation: According to NCERT, everything available in our environment which can be used to satisfy our needs is a resource, provided it is technologically accessible, economically feasible, and culturally acceptable.
questions.section: Section B: Geography (Contemporary India II)

questions.question: What is the key technical difference between 'Stock' and 'Reserves' in resource classification?
options: Stock is owned by individuals, while Reserves are owned by international bodies

Stock consists of materials that have potential to satisfy needs but lack appropriate extraction technology, whereas Reserves are a subset of stock that can be put to use with existing technology but are conserved for the future
Stock is always renewable, while Reserves are always non-renewable
Stock is found only in oceans, while Reserves are on land
questions.explanation: Materials in the environment for which we lack technology (e.g. splitting water into hydrogen fuel economically) are 'Stock'. 'Reserves' are resources where technological know-how exists, but utilization is deferred for future needs (e.g. unharnessed river water in dams).
questions.section: Section B: Geography (Contemporary India II)

questions.question: Assertion (A): Resources are not free gifts of nature, but a function of human activities.\nReason (R): Human beings interact with nature through technology and create institutions to accelerate their economic development, transforming environmental materials into resources.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
(A) is true, but (R) is false.
(A) is false, but (R) is true.
questions.explanation: Materials in nature only become resources through human knowledge, technological capability, and institutional organization. Both statements are true and (R) correctly explains (A).
questions.section: Section B: Geography (Contemporary India II)

questions.question: What is 'Biodiversity' or 'Biological Diversity'?
options: The immense variety of flora and fauna, diverse in form and function, closely integrated in a system through networks of interdependencies
The total number of domestic cattle in a village
The commercial timber exported from national forests
The artificial planting of identical eucalyptus trees
questions.explanation: Biodiversity refers to the diverse varieties of plants and animals co-existing in an ecosystem, interconnected through complex ecological webs of interdependence.
questions.section: Section B: Geography (Contemporary India II)

questions.question: During the colonial period, how did 'enrichment plantations' damage forest biodiversity in India?
options: They covered all forests with concrete
A single commercially valuable tree species was extensively planted, systematically eliminating other natural forest species (e.g. Teak in South India and Chir Pine in the Himalayas)
They introduced dangerous carnivorous predators
They poisoned all natural freshwater streams
questions.explanation: Colonial 'scientific forestry' prioritized timber profits: single commercial species like Teak monocultures in South India or Chir Pine in the Himalayas displaced diverse natural broadleaved ecosystems.
questions.section: Section B: Geography (Contemporary India II)

questions.question: Assertion (A): Human beings along with all living organisms form a complex web of ecological system in which we are only a part.\nReason (R): We are very much dependent on this system for our own existence because plants, animals, and micro-organisms recreate the quality of the air we breathe, the water we drink, and the soil that produces our food.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
(A) is true, but (R) is false.
(A) is false, but (R) is true.
questions.explanation: Human survival depends fundamentally on the ecological services rendered by flora, fauna, and decomposers. Both statements are true and (R) correctly explains (A).
questions.section: Section B: Geography (Contemporary India II)

questions.question: What percentage of the total volume of global water is estimated to exist as fresh water?
options: About 15 percent
Nearly 50 percent
96.5 percent
Only 2.5 percent
questions.explanation:
Global Water Resource Distribution (NCERT Chapter 3 Water Resources):
• Total Global Volume: 96.5% of the total volume of world's water is estimated to exist as saline ocean and sea water, which is unfit for direct human consumption, agriculture, or industrial processing.
• Freshwater Proportion: Only about 2.5% of the earth's water exists as fresh water.
• Availability Breakdown of Freshwater: Nearly 70% of this fresh water is locked up in permanent ice sheets and glaciers in Antarctica, Greenland, and mountainous regions; slightly less than 30% is stored as groundwater in aquifers. Less than 1% exists in accessible rivers and freshwater lakes.
This stark scarcity underscores why rainwater harvesting and conservation are critical. Correct option is (d).
questions.section: Section B: Geography (Contemporary India II)

questions.question: Why does regulating and damming rivers cause excessive sedimentation at the bottom of the reservoir?
options: Fish in the reservoir dig up the riverbed
Dams pump sand from the ocean into the reservoir
The dam impedes natural downstream silt flow, causing sediment to settle in the reservoir and resulting in rockier downstream river beds
Sedimentation is caused exclusively by acid rain
questions.explanation: Dams obstruct natural sediment transport; heavy silts and gravels settle at the reservoir bed, starving downstream river reaches of silt and transforming riverbeds into rocky habitats.
questions.section: Section B: Geography (Contemporary India II)

questions.subtopic: Water Scarcity in Abundant Rainfall Regions
questions.question: Assertion (A): Water scarcity may occur even in areas that receive ample annual rainfall.\nReason (R): Over-exploitation, excessive consumption, unequal access, and contamination by domestic and industrial wastes can make water unfit for human use.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
(A) is true, but (R) is false.
(A) is false, but (R) is true.
questions.explanation: Water scarcity is qualitative as well as quantitative: pollution and mismanaged consumption can cause severe water stress in regions with heavy rainfall (such as Cherrapunji or urban centers). Both are true and (R) explains (A).
questions.section: Section B: Geography (Contemporary India II)

questions.question: In the North-Eastern states of India (Assam, Meghalaya, Mizoram, and Nagaland), primitive slash-and-burn subsistence farming is commonly known as:
options: Bewar
Podu
Jhumming
Pamlou
questions.explanation:
Nomenclature of Shifting Cultivation (Jhumming):
Primitive subsistence agriculture, also known as 'slash and burn' agriculture, is a traditional system where farmers clear a patch of forest land, burn the vegetation to enrich the soil with potash ash, and cultivate food crops until fertility declines.
Regional Terms in India:
• 'Jhumming' in North-Eastern states: Assam, Meghalaya, Mizoram, and Nagaland.
• 'Pamlou' in Manipur.
• 'Dipa' in Bastar district of Chhattisgarh and Andaman & Nicobar Islands.
• 'Bewar' or 'Dahiya' in Madhya Pradesh.
• 'Podu' or 'Penda' in Andhra Pradesh.
• 'Kuruwa' in Jharkhand.
Hence, in Assam, Meghalaya, and Nagaland, it is called Jhumming. Correct option is (c).
questions.section: Section B: Geography (Contemporary India II)

questions.question: Which of the following regional names of slash-and-burn farming in India is correctly matched?
options: Dipa - Bastar district (Chhattisgarh), Podu - Andhra Pradesh, Valre - Rajasthan
Bewar - Kerala, Khil - Tamil Nadu
Jhumming - Punjab, Kuruwa - Gujarat
Pama Dabi - Maharashtra, Bringa - Haryana
questions.explanation:
Regional Matching of Slash-and-Burn Cultivation:
• Dipa: Bastar district of Chhattisgarh and Andaman & Nicobar Islands (Correct).
• Podu or Penda: Andhra Pradesh (Correct).
• Valre or Waltre: South-eastern Rajasthan (Correct).
Analysis of Incorrect Combinations:
• Bewar is in Madhya Pradesh, NOT Kerala.
• Khil is in the Himalayan belt, NOT Tamil Nadu.
• Kuruwa is in Jharkhand, NOT Gujarat.
Option (a) presents the verified, accurate NCERT geographical pairings. Correct option is (a).
questions.section: Section B: Geography (Contemporary India II)

questions.question: In Indian intensive subsistence agriculture, how has the traditional 'right of inheritance' created severe structural difficulties for farmers?
options: It forces all children to leave the village
It transfers all agricultural land to urban municipal corporations
It makes purchasing seeds illegal for younger sons
It has led to progressive fragmentation of landholdings across generations, rendering plots too small, scattered, and uneconomic to farm efficiently
questions.explanation: Continuous division of parental land among successive heirs over generations has reduced plot sizes below economic thresholds, driving intense input pressure on tiny plots.
questions.section: Section B: Geography (Contemporary India II)

questions.question: Assertion (A): Agriculture is the backbone of the Indian economic system.\nReason (R): Two-thirds of India's population is engaged in agricultural activities, and agriculture produces essential food grains as well as raw materials for various agro-based industries.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
(A) is true, but (R) is false.
(A) is false, but (R) is true.
questions.explanation: Because a massive majority of Indians derive their livelihood from farming and agriculture supplies raw materials to major industries (textiles, sugar, jute), agriculture forms the foundation of the economy. Both are true and (R) explains (A).
questions.section: Section B: Geography (Contemporary India II)

questions.question: In igneous and metamorphic rocks, minerals may occur in the cracks, crevices, faults, or joints. Smaller occurrences are called veins and larger ones are called:
options: Placer deposits
Lodes
Beds
Layers
questions.explanation: In igneous and metamorphic rocks, minerals are forced upwards in molten or gaseous forms, solidifying in fissures. Minor cracks are called veins and major formations are called lodes.
questions.section: Section B: Geography (Contemporary India II)

questions.question: The famous Monazite sands of which coastal state are rich in Thorium, a valuable nuclear fuel mineral?
options: Gujarat
West Bengal
Punjab
Kerala
questions.explanation:
Thorium Occurrence in Monazite Placer Sands:
Monazite is a reddish-brown phosphate mineral containing rare-earth metals and substantial concentrations of radioactive Thorium (Th-232).
Geographical Distribution: The coastal beach placer sands of Kerala (particularly in Chavara and Kollam districts) contain the world's richest deposits of monazite sand. Waves concentrate these heavy minerals along the coastline.
Strategic Value: Thorium is a cornerstone of India's three-stage nuclear power programme (pioneered by Dr. Homi J. Bhabha) to transition from uranium to abundant domestic thorium breeder reactors. Correct option is (d).
questions.section: Section B: Geography (Contemporary India II)

questions.question: Assertion (A): Not all mineral-bearing rocks can be commercially exploited as ores.\nReason (R): For a mineral deposit to be commercially viable, the mineral concentration must be sufficiently high and the cost of extraction must be economically feasible.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
(A) is true, but (R) is false.
(A) is false, but (R) is true.
questions.explanation:
Economic Geology (Ore vs. Mineral):
An 'ore' is a naturally occurring mineral aggregate from which a commercially valuable metal can be economically extracted at a profit.
• Assertion (A): Although minerals occur widely in rocks, only deposits with adequate concentration justify commercial investment. Mining requires massive capital for excavation, beneficiation, transport, and smelting. If mineral content is too low or extraction too costly, the rock remains a mere geological occurrence, not an ore.
• Reason (R): Accurately defines the economic parameters of ore viability: high grade, sufficient volume, and low production cost relative to market price.
Conclusion: Reason (R) correctly explains Assertion (A). Correct option is (a).
questions.section: Section B: Geography (Contemporary India II)

questions.question: Production of goods in large quantities after processing from raw materials to more valuable products is called:
options: Agriculture
Manufacturing
Tertiary distribution
Mining
questions.explanation: Production of goods in large quantities after processing from raw materials to more valuable products is called manufacturing. It falls under the secondary sector of the economy.
questions.section: Section B: Geography (Contemporary India II)

questions.question:
Assertion (A): Agriculture and industry in India are not exclusive of each other; they move hand in hand.
Reason (R): Agro-industries have given a major boost to agriculture by raising its productivity, while agricultural raw materials feed industrial manufacturing.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
(A) is true, but (R) is false.
(A) is false, but (R) is true.
questions.explanation: Agriculture and industry depend on each other. Industries depend on agriculture for raw materials and sell products like irrigation pumps, fertilisers, insecticides, pesticides, and PVC pipes to farmers, raising agricultural productivity.
questions.section: Section B: Geography (Contemporary India II)

questions.question: Efficient and rapid movement of goods, services, and people over space is a prerequisite for fast development. Hence, which sector is termed as the 'lifeline' of a national economy?
options: Transport and communication
Cottage handicraft weaving
Subsistence agriculture
Commercial advertising
questions.explanation: Transport, communication, and trade are complementary to each other. Together, they facilitate economic exchange, integrate distant regions, and act as the lifelines of our economy.
questions.section: Section B: Geography (Contemporary India II)

questions.question:
Assertion (A): Dense and efficient networks of transport and communication are a prerequisite for local, national, and global trade.
Reason (R): Today, the world has been converted into a large global village with the help of efficient and fast-moving transport systems.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
(A) is true, but (R) is false.
(A) is false, but (R) is true.
questions.explanation: Modern transport and communication technologies have transformed isolated regions into an integrated global marketplace, making them indispensable for trade and socio-economic progress.
questions.section: Section B: Geography (Contemporary India II)

questions.question: In Belgium, what percentage of the total population lives in the Flemish region and speaks the Dutch language?
options: 40 percent
80 percent
20 percent
59 percent
questions.explanation: Of the country's total population, 59 percent lives in the Flemish region and speaks Dutch language. Another 40 percent people live in the Wallonia region and speak French. The remaining 1 percent of the Belgians speak German.
questions.section: Section C: Political Science (Democratic Politics II)

questions.question: In the capital city of Belgium, Brussels, what was the special linguistic composition that created tension?
options: 100% of the population spoke only German
Dutch speakers were the overwhelming majority with 95% share
80% people spoke French while 20% spoke Dutch, reversing the national majority
English was the sole mother tongue of all citizens
questions.explanation: In Brussels, 80 percent of the people speak French while 20 percent are Dutch-speaking. The Dutch-speaking people constituted a majority in the country, but a minority in the capital.
questions.section: Section C: Political Science (Democratic Politics II)

questions.question: Why did the French-speaking community in Brussels accept equal representation in the capital city's government?
options: Because French speakers were legally forced by the European Union court
Because the Dutch community agreed to pay all national income taxes
Because Brussels was placed under direct rule of the German monarchy
Because the Dutch-speaking community had accepted equal representation in the Central Government despite being a national majority
questions.explanation: Brussels has a separate government in which both the communities have equal representation. The French-speaking people accepted equal representation in Brussels because the Dutch-speaking community has accepted equal representation in the Central Government.
questions.section: Section C: Political Science (Democratic Politics II)

questions.subtopic: A-R: Power Sharing and Social Harmony
questions.question:
Assertion (A): Power sharing is good for democracies because it helps reduce the possibility of conflict between social groups.
Reason (R): Since social conflict often leads to violence and political instability, power sharing is a good way to ensure the stability of political order.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
(A) is true, but (R) is false.
(A) is false, but (R) is true.
questions.explanation: Power sharing prevents alienation of social groups, averts violent unrest, and fosters long-term political stability, representing the prudential logic of democracy.
questions.section: Section C: Political Science (Democratic Politics II)

questions.question: Federalism is a system of government in which power is divided between:
options: A central authority and various constituent units of the country
The military high command and police forces
Different multinational corporations
The head of state and judicial magistrates only
questions.explanation:
Constitutional Definition of Federalism (NCERT Chapter 2 Federalism):
Federalism is an institutional system of shared rule and self-rule in which governmental power is constitutionally divided between a central authority (national government) and various constituent regional units (such as states or provinces).
Key Characteristics:
1. Two or more tiers of government (Union, State, and Local Panchayats/Municipalities).
2. Each tier has its own jurisdiction in specific matters of legislation, taxation, and administration specified in the Constitution.
3. Fundamental constitutional provisions cannot be unilaterally altered by one level of government.
4. Courts (Supreme Court) act as an umpire to interpret the Constitution and resolve disputes between levels. Correct option is (a).
questions.section: Section C: Political Science (Democratic Politics II)

questions.question: How does a federal system differ fundamentally from a unitary system of government?
options: In a federal system, there are no regional courts or state police
In a federal system, state governments have constitutional powers of their own for which they are not answerable to the central government
In a unitary system, power is divided equally between 50 independent states
In a federal system, the central government can dissolve state legislatures at its whim
questions.explanation: Under the unitary system, either there is only one level of government or the sub-units are subordinate to the central government. In a federal system, the central government cannot order the state government to do something unconstitutional within its jurisdiction; both governments are separately answerable to the people.
questions.section: Section C: Political Science (Democratic Politics II)

questions.question: The decision-making body of a village panchayat, consisting of all adult voters of the village who meet at least twice or thrice a year, is called the:
options: Nyaya Panchayat
Zilla Parishad
Gram Sabha
Block Samiti
questions.explanation: The Gram Panchayat works under the overall supervision of the Gram Sabha. All the voters in the village are its members. It has to meet at least twice or thrice in a year to approve the annual budget and review performance.
questions.section: Section C: Political Science (Democratic Politics II)

questions.question:
Assertion (A): The creation of linguistic States has made India more united and administration much easier.
Reason (R): Forming states on the basis of language satisfied regional aspirations and eliminated fears of forced cultural subjugation.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
(A) is true, but (R) is false.
(A) is false, but (R) is true.
questions.explanation:
Linguistic Reorganisation of Indian States (1956 Onwards):
Historical Context: When the demand for states on the basis of language was raised after Independence, national leaders feared it would lead to balkanization and disintegration of India.
Outcome of the States Reorganisation Act (1956):
Contrary to initial apprehensions, creating linguistic states (e.g. Andhra Pradesh for Telugu, Maharashtra for Marathi, Gujarat for Gujarati) accommodated deep regional identities, reduced ethnic friction, democratized governance by enabling administration in regional languages, and made the country more cohesive.
Conclusion: Assertion (A) is true, and Reason (R) provides the exact sociological explanation for why linguistic states consolidated national unity. Correct option is (a).
questions.section: Section C: Political Science (Democratic Politics II)

questions.question: A system in which all work inside the home is either done by the women of the family, or organised by them through domestic helpers, is termed:
options: Occupational mobility
Feminist hierarchy
Secular division
Sexual division of labour
questions.explanation: Sexual division of labour is a system in which all work inside the home is either done by the women of the family, or organised by them through domestic helpers.
questions.section: Section C: Political Science (Democratic Politics II)

questions.question: Movements aimed at achieving equal rights, voting franchise, educational access, and career opportunities for women are known as:
options: Feminist movements
Communal movements
Secular movements
Universal franchise movements
questions.explanation:
Sociological Definition (Feminist Movement):
A woman or a man who believes in equal rights and opportunities for women and men is termed a feminist.
Feminist Movements: Political, cultural, and social movements that campaigned for women's suffrage (voting franchise), equal legal status, enhanced educational access, workplace non-discrimination, equal pay for equal work, and autonomy in personal and domestic life.
Other terms:
• Communalism: Exploiting religious differences to mobilize political power against other communities.
• Secularism: State neutrality regarding all religions, guaranteeing no official religion. Correct option is (a).
questions.section: Section C: Political Science (Democratic Politics II)

questions.question: A feminist analysis highlighted in NCERT shows that although women constitute half of humanity, their public role is minimal because:
options: Women are legally prohibited from working in banks and offices
Men perform 90% of all household washing and cooking in rural areas
Their domestic labour (cooking, cleaning, caregiving) is unpaid, undervalued, and not accounted for in national income statistics
Women refuse to participate in higher education
questions.explanation: Although women constitute half of humanity, their role in public life, especially politics, is minimal in most societies. Their household work is invisible, unpaid, and socially devalued.
questions.section: Section C: Political Science (Democratic Politics II)

questions.question:
Assertion (A): Gender division is not based on biology but on social expectations and stereotypes.
Reason (R): Society trains boys and girls from childhood to believe that the main responsibility of women is housework and child rearing, while men work outside.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
(A) is true, but (R) is false.
(A) is false, but (R) is true.
questions.explanation: Gender division is a form of hierarchical social division seen everywhere, but it is not based on biology; it is socially constructed through cultural conditioning and sexual division of labour.
questions.section: Section C: Political Science (Democratic Politics II)

questions.question: A political party is defined as a group of people who come together to:
options: Organize religious festivals and pilgrimages
Contest elections and hold power in the government
Operate private commercial transport networks
Provide judicial arbitration in civil disputes
questions.explanation: A political party is a group of people who come together to contest elections and hold power in the government. They agree on some policies and programmes for the society with a view to promote the collective good.
questions.section: Section C: Political Science (Democratic Politics II)

questions.subtopic: Three Components of a Political Party
questions.question: A political party has three core components. Which of the following correctly identifies all three?
options: The prime minister, the supreme court judges, and the police
The president, the governor, and the chief election commissioner
The civil servants, the army generals, and the media reporters
The leaders, the active members, and the followers
questions.explanation:
Tripartite Structure of Political Parties (NCERT Chapter 6 Political Parties):
A political party is a group of people who come together to contest elections and hold power in the government. Every political party has three core structural components:
1. The Leaders: Elected or appointed officials who formulate party ideology, guide political strategy, and hold executive office when elected.
2. The Active Members: Cadres, grassroots workers, and committee delegates who organize rallies, canvas voters, and execute campaign programs.
3. The Followers: Citizens and sympathizers who endorse the party's ideological platform and vote for its candidates in elections.
Option (d) correctly lists all three statutory components.
questions.section: Section C: Political Science (Democratic Politics II)

questions.question: The Constitution was amended (52nd Amendment) to introduce the Anti-Defection Law primarily to prevent:
options: Elected MLAs and MPs from changing parties after being elected in order to become ministers or for cash payoffs
Voters from casting negative votes in elections
New political parties from registering with the Election Commission
Judges from hearing election petition cases
questions.explanation: The Constitution was amended to prevent elected MLAs and MPs from changing parties. This was done because many elected representatives were indulging in defection in order to become ministers or for cash rewards. Now the law says that if any MLA or MP changes parties, he or she will lose the seat in the legislature.
questions.section: Section C: Political Science (Democratic Politics II)

questions.question:
Assertion (A): Modern representative democracies cannot exist without political parties.
Reason (R): Political parties aggregate diverse public opinions into coherent policy directions, form accountable governments, and provide a legitimate opposition.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
(A) is true, but (R) is false.
(A) is false, but (R) is true.
questions.explanation:
Indispensability of Political Parties in Modern Democracy:
Assertion (A): Without political parties, every candidate in an election would be an independent individual. No one would be able to make any unified national policy promises to the electorate. The government might be formed, but its utility would remain ever uncertain.
Reason (R): Political parties perform the indispensable democratic function of interest aggregation—synthesizing millions of diverse individual opinions into actionable public policies. They formulate governments, provide an organized institutional opposition to keep the ruling party accountable, and give voters a clear choice between competing governance philosophies.
Conclusion: Reason (R) directly explains why representative democracies cannot function without political parties. Correct option is (a).
questions.section: Section C: Political Science (Democratic Politics II)

questions.question: Which of the following is widely accepted as a core principle demonstrating why democracy is superior to non-democratic regimes?
options: It eliminates the need for national defense spending completely
It guarantees uniform wealth distribution within two fiscal quarters
It promotes equality among citizens and enhances the dignity of the individual
It allows executive heads to rule without any parliamentary consultation
questions.explanation: Democracy is considered a better form of government because it promotes equality among citizens, enhances individual dignity, improves decision quality, provides conflict resolution mechanisms, and allows room to correct mistakes.
questions.section: Section C: Political Science (Democratic Politics II)

questions.question: In a democratic government, to whom are elected rulers fundamentally accountable?
options: Only to the international monetary institutions
To the citizens and electorate who vote them into power
To hereditary feudal landholders
To supreme military commanders
questions.explanation: In a democracy, we are most concerned with ensuring that people will have the right to choose their rulers and people will have control over the rulers. Whenever possible, citizens should participate in decision-making.
questions.section: Section C: Political Science (Democratic Politics II)

questions.question: When examining the actual record of democracies on being 'responsive to the needs and demands of the people', what does historical evidence suggest?
options: Democracies fulfill 100% of all citizen requests within 24 hours of petitioning
Democracies often frustrate the needs of the people and frequently ignore the demands of a majority of their population
Democracies are immune to corruption and bribery at all bureaucratic tiers
Democracies never experience worker strikes or civic demonstrations
questions.explanation: The record of democracies is not impressive on responsiveness: democracies often frustrate the needs of the people and often ignore the demands of a majority of its population. The routine tales of corruption are enough to convince that democracy is not free of this evil.
questions.section: Section C: Political Science (Democratic Politics II)

questions.question:
Assertion (A): Democratic governments take more time to take decisions compared to authoritarian regimes.
Reason (R): Democratic decision-making is based on consultation, negotiation, and adherence to established constitutional procedures.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
(A) is true, but (R) is false.
(A) is false, but (R) is true.
questions.explanation: Democracy is based on deliberation and negotiation. Because it follows norms and procedures, decision-making takes time, but the decisions are more acceptable and effective.
questions.section: Section C: Political Science (Democratic Politics II)

questions.question: Which of the following statements best illustrates that 'different people can have different developmental goals'?
options: A prosperous Punjab farmer seeks higher minimum support prices, while a landless rural labourer seeks more days of work and better daily wages
All citizens in a country have mathematically identical aspirations for economic progress
Industrialists and adivasi tribals always agree on building mega hydroelectric dams
Urban unemployed youth seek identical developmental policies as rural subsistence farmers
questions.explanation: Different persons can have different developmental goals because their life situations differ. A prosperous farmer wants high support prices for crops and cheap labour, whereas a landless labourer wants more days of work, better wages, and quality local schooling for children.
questions.section: Section D: Economics (Understanding Economic Development)

questions.question: What may be development for an industrialist who desires more electricity by constructing large dams may be destructive for:
options: Multinational power transmission corporations
Turbine and heavy electrical machinery manufacturers
Local tribal communities and farmers whose lands and homes are submerged by the reservoir
Urban factory owners seeking reliable electrical grid supplies
questions.explanation: To get more electricity, industrialists may want more dams. But this may submerge the land and disrupt the lives of people who are displaced — such as tribals. Thus, what may be development for one may not be development for the other; it may even be destructive for the other.
questions.section: Section D: Economics (Understanding Economic Development)

questions.question: A metropolitan city plans a high-speed elevated highway corridor. This project benefits private car owners by cutting commute times, but destroys the shops and livelihoods of roadside vendors and small shopkeepers. This scenario demonstrates:
options: Elevated expressways eliminate poverty for all citizens automatically
Roadside vendors should be barred from using judicial courts
Urban planning is legally exempted from constitutional review
Developmental goals can be mutually conflicting; what represents development for one section can cause economic displacement for another
questions.explanation: People have conflicting developmental goals. An urban commuter benefits from elevated flyovers, but small roadside vendors lose their shops and livelihoods when land is acquired, creating conflict between different social groups.
questions.section: Section D: Economics (Understanding Economic Development)

questions.question: A young engineer is offered two jobs: Job A offers very high pay but no job security and long erratic hours leaving no time for family; Job B offers slightly lower pay but regular hours, permanent job security, and health insurance for family. If she chooses Job B, it proves that:
options: High salaries are legally prohibited in private software corporations
Engineers are irrational economic decision makers
Job security is irrelevant to modern professionals
People look at a mix of goals including job security, working environment, and work-life balance, not just monetary salary alone
questions.explanation: If women or men are engaged in paid work, their dignity increases. But people look at a mix of goals: working environment, opportunity to learn, sense of security, and freedom are as critical as monetary salary.
questions.section: Section D: Economics (Understanding Economic Development)

questions.question:
Assertion (A): Per Capita Income is not a comprehensive indicator of human development.
Reason (R): Per Capita Income measures only average monetary income and fails to capture disparities in distribution, healthcare, or educational attainment.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
(A) is true, but (R) is false.
(A) is false, but (R) is true.
questions.explanation:
Economics: Limitations of Per Capita Income (NCERT Chapter 1 Development):
Per Capita Income (Average Income = National Income / Total Population) is widely used by the World Bank in its World Development Reports, but it has severe structural limitations:
1. Conceals Income Disparities: A country with an elite few earning billions and millions living in extreme poverty can have the same average per capita income as an egalitarian society where wealth is evenly distributed.
2. Neglects Non-Material Dimensions: It tells us nothing about literacy rates, infant mortality rates, life expectancy, clean drinking water access, gender parity, or environmental sustainability.
This is why the UNDP Human Development Index (HDI) integrates health (life expectancy) and education (mean years of schooling) alongside per capita income. Reason (R) correctly explains Assertion (A). Correct option is (a).
questions.section: Section D: Economics (Understanding Economic Development)

questions.question: Economic activities that involve exploiting natural resources directly (such as agriculture, dairy, fishing, and forestry) belong to the:
options: Primary Sector
Secondary Sector
Tertiary Sector
Quaternary Sector
questions.explanation: When we produce a good by exploiting natural resources, it is an activity of the primary sector. This is because it forms the base for all other products that we subsequently make.
questions.section: Section D: Economics (Understanding Economic Development)

questions.question: The sector that covers activities in which natural products are changed into other forms through manufacturing processes associated with industrial activity is the:
options: Primary Sector
Secondary Sector (Industrial Sector)
Tertiary Sector
Agrarian Sector
questions.explanation: The secondary sector covers activities in which natural products are changed into other forms through ways of manufacturing that we associate with industrial activity. For example, using sugarcane as a raw material to make sugar or gur.
questions.section: Section D: Economics (Understanding Economic Development)

questions.question: If all truck drivers and transport operators across India decide to go on a nationwide strike, what immediate economic consequence will follow?
options: The agricultural sector will automatically double its food grain output
Software companies will begin manufacturing heavy diesel trucks
Farmers will be unable to sell their vegetables and milk, causing produce to rot, while urban factories shut down due to lack of raw materials
Wholesale commodity prices in urban retail markets will drop to zero
questions.explanation: This demonstrates sectoral interdependence: the tertiary sector (transport) links primary agricultural producers to urban consumers and secondary factory processors. Without transport, both primary and secondary sectors collapse.
questions.citation: NCERT Class 10 Economics, Chapter 2, Section 2.1 (Table on Interdependence)
questions.section: Section D: Economics (Understanding Economic Development)

questions.question: A farmer cultivates raw cotton (Primary), a textile mill spins yarn and weaves cloth (Secondary), and a wholesale trader transports and markets the shirts to retail stores (Tertiary). This value chain proves that:
options: Economic sectors do not function in isolation; each successive sector adds economic value to the output of preceding sectors
Raw cotton can be converted into shirts without any industrial processing
Wholesale traders belong exclusively to the primary agricultural sector
Secondary manufacturing can operate without raw materials from nature
questions.explanation: Each stage in the supply chain builds upon the preceding stage: primary provides raw natural fibre, secondary transforms it into fabric and garments, and tertiary distributes it to the consumer.
questions.section: Section D: Economics (Understanding Economic Development)

questions.subtopic: A-R: Counting Final Goods in GDP
questions.question:
Assertion (A): While computing the Gross Domestic Product (GDP), only the value of final goods and services is considered.
Reason (R): Intermediate goods are completely consumed during the production process and their monetary value is already reflected in the market price of the final good.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
(A) is true, but (R) is false.
(A) is false, but (R) is true.
questions.explanation: Intermediate goods like flour and sugar are absorbed into final goods like biscuits; counting intermediate goods separately would cause the error of double counting.
questions.section: Section D: Economics (Understanding Economic Development)

questions.question: In a barter economy where goods are directly exchanged without the use of money, which essential condition must be satisfied?
options: A formal promissory guarantee certified by the village panchayat
Gold coins deposited with an escrow magistrate
Double coincidence of wants (both parties must agree to sell and buy each other's commodities)
A fixed exchange price list published by the state government
questions.explanation: Double coincidence of wants is an essential feature of a barter economy. What a person desires to sell is exactly what the other wishes to buy. Money eliminates the need for double coincidence of wants by acting as an intermediate medium of exchange.
questions.section: Section D: Economics (Understanding Economic Development)

questions.question: Why is money referred to as a 'medium of exchange'?
options: Because it is minted exclusively from precious silver and gold bullion
Because it acts as an intermediary instrument in the transactions and exchange of goods and services
Because it can only be exchanged inside foreign diplomatic embassies
Because it changes its face value automatically every month
questions.explanation: Since money acts as an intermediate in the exchange process, it is called a medium of exchange. A person holding money can easily exchange it for any commodity or service that he or she might want.
questions.section: Section D: Economics (Understanding Economic Development)

questions.question: A shoe manufacturer wants to sell shoes and buy wheat. In a barter system without money, what difficulty does he immediately encounter?
options: He must obtain an export license from the United Nations
He is legally prohibited from consuming wheat products
He can only trade with merchants who speak foreign languages
He must find a wheat-growing farmer who not only wants to sell wheat, but also wants to buy the exact size and style of shoes he makes
questions.explanation: Both parties have to agree to sell and buy each other's commodities. If the farmer wants clothes instead of shoes, no exchange can occur — the classic obstacle of double coincidence of wants.
questions.section: Section D: Economics (Understanding Economic Development)

questions.question: What would happen to a commercial bank if all of its depositors arrive on the exact same morning demanding to withdraw their entire savings in cash?
options: The bank would immediately double its profits by collecting withdrawal fees
The bank would print new paper currency in its back office within ten minutes
The bank manager would be declared the permanent governor of the Reserve Bank
The bank would face a liquidity crisis ('bank run') and be unable to pay all depositors immediately because most funds are tied up in long-term loans
questions.explanation: Because banks keep only about 15% cash reserves based on the statistical assumption that not all depositors withdraw money on the same day, a simultaneous mass withdrawal causes a run on the bank.
questions.section: Section D: Economics (Understanding Economic Development)

questions.subtopic: A-R: Money as Medium of Exchange
questions.question:
Assertion (A): Money eliminates the necessity for double coincidence of wants in an economy.
Reason (R): Money acts as a universal intermediate medium in the exchange process, allowing individuals to trade commodities without reciprocal barter needs.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
(A) is true, but (R) is false.
(A) is false, but (R) is true.
questions.explanation:
Monetary Economics: Elimination of Double Coincidence of Wants:
Barter Bottleneck: In a barter economy without money, trade requires a 'double coincidence of wants'—what a seller wishes to sell must coincide exactly with what a buyer wishes to purchase. If an apple farmer wants shoes, he must find a shoemaker who simultaneously desires apples.
Role of Money: Money acts as an intermediate medium of exchange. A person holding money can easily exchange it for any commodity or service in the market. Since transactions are split into two independent steps (sale for money, then purchase with money), the cumbersome double coincidence requirement is eliminated.
Conclusion: Reason (R) accurately explains the operational mechanism behind Assertion (A). Correct option is (a).
questions.section: Section D: Economics (Understanding Economic Development)

questions.question: A Multinational Corporation (MNC) is defined as a company that:
options: Owns or controls production of goods and services in more than one nation
Operates exclusively within a single municipal district
Is owned and directed by the United Nations General Assembly
Produces goods exclusively for non-profit charitable donation
questions.explanation: A Multinational Corporation (MNC) is a company that owns or controls production in more than one nation. MNCs set up offices and factories for production in regions where they can get cheap labour and other resources.
questions.section: Section D: Economics (Understanding Economic Development)

questions.subtopic: Why MNCs Set Up Production Globally
questions.question: Why do MNCs locate their production units in different countries across the globe?
options: To distribute 100% of their revenues as free aid to foreign citizens
Because their home countries have legally banned all factory manufacturing
To minimise the cost of production and maximise their profits by leveraging cheap labour, resources, and proximity to markets
To avoid communicating with international transport companies
questions.explanation: MNCs set up production where it is close to the markets; where there is skilled and unskilled labour available at low costs; and where the availability of other factors of production is assured. This is done so that the cost of production is low and the MNCs can earn greater profits.
questions.section: Section D: Economics (Understanding Economic Development)

questions.subtopic: Joint Ventures: Ford Motors in India
questions.question: In 1995, American automobile giant Ford Motors entered the Indian market through a joint venture with Mahindra & Mahindra. What mutual benefit did this joint venture deliver?
options: Ford took over the entire railway network of the Indian government
Ford brought global manufacturing technology and capital, while Mahindra provided established domestic component sourcing, dealership networks, and market knowledge
Mahindra was forced to cease all manufacturing operations in India
Ford produced cars exclusively for donation to rural hospitals
questions.explanation: Joint ventures combine local company assets (distribution networks, component vendors, local market understanding) with MNC capital and advanced production technology.
questions.section: Section D: Economics (Understanding Economic Development)

questions.question: To attract foreign MNC investments, governments in India have permitted 'flexibility in labour laws'. How has this directly affected factory workers?
options: Workers are increasingly hired on short-term contractual basis during peak seasons without job security, paid sick leave, or provident fund benefits
Workers receive permanent lifetime employment contracts with double wages
Workers are appointed as permanent members of company boards of directors
Workers are legally exempt from working more than four hours a week
questions.explanation: In recent years, the government has allowed companies to ignore many labour laws to reduce costs. Instead of hiring workers on a regular basis, companies hire workers 'flexibly' for short periods when there is intense pressure of work, eroding job security.
questions.section: Section D: Economics (Understanding Economic Development)

questions.question:
Assertion (A): Multinational Corporations disperse different stages of manufacturing across multiple nations rather than producing in a single country.
Reason (R): Dispersing production allows MNCs to exploit specific locational advantages (cheap labour, specialized engineering, proximity to markets) to minimize total production costs.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
(A) is true, but (R) is false.
(A) is false, but (R) is true.
questions.explanation:
Globalisation: Global Dispersion of MNC Production:
Strategy of Multinational Corporations (MNCs):
MNCs set up production facilities not in a single country, but across regions where production costs are lowest and market access is highest.
Example (NCERT Illustration):
A large MNC producing industrial equipment designs its products in specialized research centers in the United States, manufactures complex components in China (where low-cost manufacturing infrastructure exists), ships them to Mexico and Eastern Europe for assembly close to major consumer markets in North America and Europe, and manages global technical customer support through English-speaking call centers in India.
This spatial fragmentation allows MNCs to minimize production costs by up to 50–60%. Reason (R) correctly explains Assertion (A). Correct option is (a).
questions.section: Section D: Economics (Understanding Economic Development)
